title: Land is not a commodity: why a land value tax can cure the housing crisis
dek: The housing shortage is only the surface; the real disease is land monopoly: a land value tax shifts the burden from buildings to land, forcing hoarders to develop or sell, returning location value to society instead of enriching landlords.
why: The land value tax is an overlooked lever that both left- and right-wing economists agree on. Lars Doucet uses cases like Houston parking lots, Korea's assessment system, and Norway's resource dividend to turn an abstract tax into a story of power.
who: Economists concerned with housing policy, urban planners, real estate developers, and investors and policy researchers wondering whether a land tax is worth betting on.

points.h: A land tax is not a property tax; it is a location tax
points.body: Lars opens with a metaphor: the land value tax shares a root with ordinary property tax but splits 'building value' from 'land value.' A building tax punishes you for building, maintaining, and renovating; a land tax punishes only occupying a prime location while letting it sit idle. He says land's value comes from the labor of those around you—the fact that you can step out and work, go to school, make friends depends on your neighbors and the whole city. Landlords lie back and siphon this collective value into their own pockets. That is the paradox of 'Progress and Poverty': a ballpoint pen fell from $270 to 11 cents, but land never does.

points.h: The build-more camp is right, but not enough
points.body: The host asks: Oakland loosened density and rents fell—do we still need a land tax? Lars concedes the 'housing shortage' is the main cause, but points out the YIMBYs don't explain a counterexample: Houston has no zoning, yet downtown still has a $500 million surface parking lot. Why? Because the property tax bundles land and buildings together—the more you build, the more you pay, while hoarding and waiting for appreciation is cheaper. So developers have no incentive to build, only to lobby for rezonings and then keep hoarding. Without a land tax, he says, reform hits the impasse of 'you changed the zoning, but I still won't sell.'

points.h: The objections are born of imagination
points.body: Lars sorts the opposition into three categories and dismantles each. How do you separate land from buildings in assessment? He says about 14,000 assessment jurisdictions worldwide already do something similar; Korea manually reviews 500,000 sample parcels a year and produces a nationwide land value map in five months; Norway trains a national automated valuation model on the Finn.no property platform with a core team of just three people. Worried about protests? He says the real source of protest is 'my land looks like my neighbor's, why am I charged more'—under a land tax, your assessment basis is the same location as your neighbor's, so it's easier to justify. The excuse for not implementing is that it hasn't been measured.

points.h: The little old lady is not a reason to object
points.body: The sharpest criticism is 'transition unfairness'—the day a land tax is announced, existing landowners instantly bear the capitalization of all future taxes, a one-time expropriation. Lars acknowledges this is a Gordon Tullock-style transition trap, then offers safeguards: action is never a one-step national 100% land tax, but a gradual switch by school district or county; run revenue-neutral simulations, and most single-family homes see their tax bill fall. As for the elderly worried about being driven out, he says Texas already has a tax deferral system: you owe it, and after death it is deducted from the estate with interest.

points.h: Britain's failure is a capacity problem
points.body: The most common counterexample online is Britain's 1910 'People's Budget': valuation took six years and was overturned by shopkeeper protests and the courts. Lars's response is blunt: the much-discussed article is 'inferring a universal law from one sample,' and simultaneously claims 'a pure land tax has never succeeded' and 'land cannot be valued'—yet Korea has been assessing national land values parcel by parcel for decades. He says this only proves Britain's state capacity was weak, not that a land tax is theoretically unworkable. His tone hardens: if you want to be a serious critic, go find counterexamples, don't pass off lazy ignorance as settled wisdom.

points.h: Norway achieves Georgism through resource dividends
points.body: Lars points to a fact that makes today's Norway a 'success story': the entire Norwegian resource management system is Georgist in structure—oil and other natural resources are deemed the property of all the people, extractors pay very high resource taxes, but production and investment themselves are not penalized, thus encouraging entrepreneurship while channeling the natural dividend into the state treasury to subsidize universal welfare. Norway's Georgism is almost perfect, except it does not apply to land value. This 'Norwegian paradox' leads him to assert: the land tax is not the enemy of the welfare state; it can be its foundation.

points.h: The automobile opened a second frontier
points.body: Lars explains why the land question that filled the air 100 years ago later disappeared: the frontier itself was a kind of 'free land' mechanism—as long as you could expand into the wilderness, the lower classes did not have to face the squeeze of 'high work plus high rent.' America's first frontier was westward expansion; after it closed came Henry George. In the 20th century, the automobile turned the suburbs into a 'second frontier,' extending the reprieve another 80 years until it closed again around 2006–2008. He says some now call it a 'second Gilded Age,' but it is just the same script from a hundred years ago with a new cast, and post-pandemic remote work as a 'third frontier' lasted about five minutes before capital absorbed it.

points.h: Don't win online; do the politicians' homework
points.body: The closing answer is practical: Lars says the most effective way he has found to create change in the past five years is not arguing with keyboard warriors, but preparing data simulations and ready answers to every objection a state senator or city councilor might raise, and putting them directly on their desks—he calls 'doing homework for politicians' an absurd but remarkably effective strategy. Several states have already passed bills allowing land value tax reforms. His advice: go measure, don't guess.

terms.def: An annual tax levied on the value of land rather than the total value of property; it does not penalize building improvements.
The movement founded by Henry George in the 19th century: land is common wealth, and ground rent should be collected for society.
The movement advocating loosening zoning restrictions and allowing more housing construction.
Using uniform models and sample parcels to automatically value all properties in a jurisdiction, rather than assessing each one individually.
The Georgist ideal: tax only land value, abolishing other taxes on labor and capital.
High rents extracted from natural resources (such as oil), owned by all citizens.
